title: Several contracts on one outcome
objectives: Make consistent markets on several contracts tied to one die, and trade the mispricing between them.

screens.title: The face if even
screens.prose: One die. Contract E pays the face if it is even, and nothing if it is odd. The bars are E's payoff on each face.
screens.question: What is E worth?

hints.text: Average E's payoff over all six faces, zeros included.
The payoffs total $2 + 4 + 6 = 12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the total payoff by all six faces.

byKey.evens: You averaged the even faces only. E pays nothing half the time, so divide by 6.
byKey.half: You halved the face's average, 3.5. The even faces are the larger ones.

explain.text: E pays 12 in total over six equally likely faces, so it is worth 2. Averaging only the even faces gives 4, which ignores the zeros. Every contract is priced over the whole die.

screens.title: One table of values
screens.prose: A pays the face, E the face if even, F the face if odd. Each row is a face. Fill the fair value of each contract.
screens.question: Fill the fair row.

hints.text: Average each column over the six faces.
A totals 21, E 12 and F 9.
Divide by 6: 3.5, 2 and 1.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each fair value is its column total over 6.

explain.text: On every row E plus F equals A, so their fair values add too: $2 + 1.5 = 3.5$. Payoffs that add face by face give prices that add. That is the rule behind every family of contracts.

screens.title: Quotes that fit together
screens.prose: The interviewer asks for markets on A, E and F, each 0.4 wide.
screens.question: Which set of quotes is consistent?

options.why: You centred E on the even faces' average. E is worth 2, not 4.
Your E sits 0.5 above fair. The interviewer sells you E at 2.3 and gains 0.3 a unit on average.

options.text: A, E and F all 3.3 to 3.7
options.why: You gave every contract A's price. E and F pay less than A on every face.

hints.text: Centre each quote on its own fair value.
Centres 3.5, 2 and 1.5.
Each 0.2 either side of its centre: E 1.8 to 2.2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Centre each quote on its fair value.

byKey.evens: You centred E on the even faces' average. E is worth 2, not 4.
byKey.skewE: Your E sits 0.5 above fair. The interviewer sells you E at 2.3 and gains 0.3 a unit on average.

explain.text: Centred on 3.5, 2 and 1.5, the quotes leave no gap to trade through. E's bid plus F's bid, 3.1, sits below A's ask; their asks, 3.9, sit above A's bid. No combination buys A cheaper than its parts.

screens.title: The interviewer's quotes
screens.prose: Now the interviewer quotes A at 3.0 to 3.2, E at 2.1 to 2.3 and F at 1.6 to 1.8. Buy A, sell E and sell F: the table shows each face.
screens.question: What do you lock in per set, in pounds?

widget.accept: £0.50: sell E at 2.1 and F at 1.6, buy A at 3.2.
widget.label: Profit per set

hints.text: You buy at the ask and sell at the bid.
Selling E and F brings in $2.1 + 1.6 = 3.7$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sell E and F at their bids, buy A at its ask.

byKey.mids: You used the mid prices. You trade at the quotes.
byKey.rev: You bought E and F at their asks and sold A at its bid.

explain.text: The position is flat on every face, so the roll does not matter. You took in 3.7 and paid 3.2: £0.50 a set. The interviewer's E and F add to more than their A.

screens.title: Dealing in E
screens.prose: You make the market in E. A trades 3.4 to 3.6 and F 1.4 to 1.6. So E = A − F can be bought for 2.2 and sold for 1.8 elsewhere. An arbitrageur, listed as `scripted`, trades against any E quote outside that band. Size 1 to 5, width 0.2 to 0.6.
screens.question: Finish the six turns with a P&L of at least £0.30 and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: You make the market in E, which pays the face of one die if it is even. The market quotes A (the face) at 3.4 to 3.6 and F (the face if odd) at 1.4 to 1.6. Other traders deal only within 0.2 of fair.

hints.text: What is E worth, from the table you filled?
E is worth 2, and the band runs from 1.8 to 2.2.
Quote 1.9 at 2.1 for 3.

feedback.correct: Your E quote sat inside the band, centred on 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Centre E on 2, inside the band 1.8 to 2.2.

byKey.low: Your P&L is under £0.30. An E quote off the band lets the arbitrageur trade against A and F.
byKey.crossed: Your bid met or passed your ask, so nobody traded.

explain.text: The model quoted 1.9 at 2.1 for 3. It sold 4 at 2.1 and bought 3 at 1.9: short 1, cash +£2.70. The die showed 2, so E settled at 2: +£0.70.

screens.title: The E ledger
screens.prose: You finished with a P&L in pounds of {{carry.cont.pnl|0}}, holding {{carry.cont.position|0}}. The table is the model run. The die showed 2, so E paid 2.

state.caption: Turns 1, 3 and 5: the arbitrageur found nothing.

screens.question: What is the model run's P&L, in pounds?

hints.text: Cash, then the short 1 settled at 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cash 2.70 less the short 1 at 2.

byKey.cash: That is the cash alone. You still owe E on the short 1.
byKey.long: You added the short as if long. Short 1 owes 2.

explain.text: The edges are +0.30, +0.10 and +0.30, which make £0.70. Quoting E alone near 4, as the opening quote does, buys 3 at 3.8: −£5.40. The family's table is what kept the quote right.

screens.title: Your own quotes, against you
screens.prose: You quote each contract on its own: A 3.3 to 3.7, E 1.4 to 1.6 and F 1.2 to 1.4. The interviewer buys E and F at your offers and sells you A at your bid, ten sets.
screens.question: What is your P&L on ten sets, in pounds?

hints.text: Is your position flat on every face?
Long A, short E and F: flat. Only the cash counts.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You are flat, so the P&L is the cash.

byKey.one: That is one set. They traded ten.
byKey.sign: You received 3.0 and paid 3.3 a set: a loss.
byKey.risk: You assumed the roll decides it. Long A against short E and F is flat on every face.

explain.text: Your E and F offers add to 3.0, below your A bid of 3.3. Each set loses £0.30 for sure, so ten lose £3.00. Quoting contracts one at a time lets the family not add up.

screens.title: The square of the face
screens.prose: Q pays the face squared, worth $91/6$. A new contract pays $(\text{face} - 3.5)^2$. Face by face it equals $Q - 7A + 12.25$.
screens.question: What is the new contract worth? Give 4 places.

hints.text: Prices add as payoffs do: price Q, A and the constant.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price it as $Q - 7A + 12.25$.

byKey.zero: You priced the face at its mean first. The square of the average is not the average of the square.
byKey.sq: You squared the distance of one middle face. Average over all six.

explain.text: $91/6 - 24.5 + 12.25 = 35/12$, the variance of one die. The column of payoffs averages $17.5/6$, which agrees. Any contract built from others is priced from their prices.

screens.title: A contract that always pays £1
screens.prose: Contract U pays £1 whatever the die shows.
screens.question: What is a sensible market in U?

options.why: You added width for risk that is not there. U pays 1 on every face.
You priced it like a bet. U never pays 0.

options.text: Around 1/6, the chance of one face
options.why: You priced one face. U pays on all six.

hints.text: How much does U pay on each face?
£1 on every face.
Nothing is uncertain, so the width can be 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. U pays the same on every face.

byKey.wide: You added width for risk that is not there. U pays 1 on every face.
byKey.half: You priced it like a bet. U never pays 0.

explain.text: U is cash, worth exactly 1, so there is nothing to be wrong about. Width pays for uncertainty, and U has none. In the table, U is the constant that lets $(\text{face} - 3.5)^2$ be built.

screens.title: One table, many contracts
screens.prose:
Write every contract's payoff on the six faces. If payoffs add face by face, fair values add the same way:
$$X = aY + bZ + c \text{ on every face} \implies \text{fair}(X) = a\,\text{fair}(Y) + b\,\text{fair}(Z) + c.$$
screens.question: H pays the face if it is 4 or more. What is it worth?

hints.text: Total H's payoff over six faces.

byKey.mean: You averaged the three high faces only.
byKey.chance: That is the chance H pays, not its value.

explain.text: H is worth 2.5, and "the face if 3 or less" is worth 1. Together they pay A on every face, and $2.5 + 1 = 3.5$. The table checks a whole family at once.

screens.title: The family in code
screens.prose: Code the table: each fair value is the average over six faces. Then check whether a combination is a true arbitrage. `PAY` holds seven contracts.
screens.question: Complete `fair_values` and `find_arb`.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction


def fair_values(contracts):
    """contracts: {name: [payoff on faces 1..6]}.
    Return {name: Fraction fair value}."""
    ...


def find_arb(payoffs, quotes, combo):
    """combo: {name: +1 to buy, -1 to sell}. Buy at the
    ask, sell at the bid (quotes: {name: (bid, ask)}).
    If the combined payoff is the same on every face,
    return that payoff plus the cash, if positive.
    Otherwise return Fraction(0)."""
    ...

tests.expect: {'A': Fraction(7, 2), 'E': Fraction(2), 'F': Fraction(3, 2), 'H': Fraction(5, 2), 'L': Fraction(1), 'U': Fraction(1), 'Q': Fraction(91, 6)}

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Values are exact Fractions. A combination that leaves risk on some face returns 0.

hints.text: The combined payoff on face f is the sum of `q * payoffs[k][f]`.
It must be the same number on all six faces.
Buying pays the ask; selling receives the bid. Add the constant payoff to the cash.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check that the payoff is constant across faces, and the sign of the cash.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that each `...` is replaced.

explain.text: Selling U at 1.1 is an arbitrage of 0.10: you owe 1 on every face. Buying H and L for 3.5 against A at 3.6 locks 0.10 too. A combination that leaves a face exposed returns 0, however good its cash.

screens.title: Strikes and the future
screens.prose: An options desk prices every strike from one model, as you priced A, E and F from one table. With no interest to discount, a call less a put at the same strike pays the future less the strike. The future is 102, and the 100 call is worth 6.
screens.question: What must the 100 put be worth?

hints.text: Call − put = future − strike.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use call − put = future − strike.

byKey.same: You priced the put like the call. The future is above the strike, so the call is worth more.
byKey.sign: You added the 2. The call is the dearer one here.

explain.text: Long call and short put pays the future less 100 on every outcome, so their prices differ by 2. A put at 4.5 would let someone sell it, buy the call and sell the future for 0.50. Lesson 17 plays this on dice.

ideas: Write every contract's payoff on the six faces, and price each as its average.
When payoffs add face by face, prices must add too: E + F = A, so 2 + 1.5 = 3.5.
Quotes that do not add up can be traded through for a sure profit, by you or against you.

formula.name: Prices follow payoffs
formula.tex: X = aY + bZ + c \implies \text{fair}(X) = a\,\text{fair}(Y) + b\,\text{fair}(Z) + c
formula.note: The equality must hold on every face.

summary.trap: Quoting each contract on its own: your E and F offers can add to less than your A bid.

quiz.prose: One die. A contract pays £1 if the face is 5 or 6.
quiz.question: What is it worth?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. It pays £1 on two faces of six.

byKey.faces: You averaged the faces. It pays £1, not the face.
byKey.half: You treated it as a coin. Two faces of six is 1/3.

explain.text: It pays 1 on faces 5 and 6, and 0 on the rest: $2/6 = 1/3$. A £1 contract is worth its chance. Its payoff column is two ones and four zeros.

quiz.prose: Quotes: A at 3.6 to 3.8, and "the face if 4 or more" at 2.3 to 2.5. "The face if 3 or less" is 0.9 to 1.0. You trade 20 sets.
quiz.question: What do you lock in, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Buy both parts at their asks, sell A at its bid, 20 times.

byKey.one: That is one set. You traded 20.
byKey.rev: You sold the parts and bought A. That loses.

explain.text: The two parts cost $2.5 + 1.0 = 3.5$ and together pay A, which sells at 3.6. Each set locks £0.10, so 20 lock £2.00. The parts' fair values, 2.5 and 1, add to A's 3.5.

quiz.prose: You must quote E, the face if even, with no table in front of you.
quiz.question: Which centre is right?

options.text: 2: the even faces total 12, over six faces

options.why: You averaged only the even faces. E pays 0 half the time.
You split A evenly. The even faces carry more of the total.
You halved the 6. Average every face.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average E over all six faces.

explain.text: E pays 2, 4 and 6 on half the faces and 0 on the rest: $12/6 = 2$. F is then $3.5 - 2 = 1.5$. One number from the table fixes the other.
